items.title: Google ML Drift Accelerates On-Device AI Inference across Diverse GPUs
items.summary_1line: Google has released ML Drift, an open-source, cross-platform GPU compute engine designed for on-device AI and machine learning inference. Licensed under Apache 2.0, it abstracts the complexities of different GPU hardw...
items.editor_note: First-party starting point: Google releases a vendor-neutral GPU engine, scoped to on-device inference.

items.title: CUDA+ROCm dual-back ends LLM inference for mixed-vendor GPUs (up to 48% faster)
items.summary_1line: CUDA+ROCm dual-back ends LLM inference for mixed-vendor GPUs (up to 48% faster)
items.editor_note: Moves the thread to datacenter LLMs: one job across NVIDIA and AMD, with a self-reported speedup claim.

items.title: Kindi: The fastest software inference engine for low-cost GPUs
items.summary_1line: Kindi: The fastest software inference engine for low-cost GPUs
items.editor_note: Adds the low-cost-GPU angle: a new engine whose "fastest" billing has no independent benchmark yet.

editorial.tldr: This is a loose thread of separate projects, not one event: each tries to run inference on GPUs beyond a single high-end CUDA stack. Google opened it with ML Drift, an Apache 2.0 engine for on-device inference across GPU vendors; a C++/HIP server for AMD GPUs and a project-maya pull request for mixed CUDA+ROCm LLM inference, titled up to 48% faster, followed.
editorial.whats_new: Kindi, a software inference engine aimed at low-cost GPUs, surfaced on Hacker News billing itself as the fastest in its class; the claim is the author's own, with no independent benchmark in the thread.
editorial.why_it_matters: Inference that runs on cheaper or non-NVIDIA GPUs gives teams leverage on hardware cost and supply, but these projects are early and every performance claim here is self-reported.
editorial.take_for_builders: Treat these as experiments: rerun your own latency and throughput evals on low-cost, mixed, or AMD hardware before you plan capacity around them, and keep your current CUDA serving path as the fallback.

beats.headline: Google open-sources ML Drift for on-device inference across GPUs
beats.summary: A first-party GPU compute engine that hides vendor differences for on-device ML inference.

beats.headline: A C++/HIP inference server targets AMD GPUs directly
beats.summary: A small independent project skips CUDA and writes the server against AMD's HIP API.

beats.headline: Dual CUDA+ROCm backend PR claims up to 48% faster mixed-vendor inference
beats.summary: An open pull request, not a release; the speedup comes from the PR title alone.

beats.headline: Kindi pitches itself as the fastest engine for low-cost GPUs
beats.summary: The angle shifts from GPU vendor to GPU price tier; the speed claim is unverified.

open_questions: Does Kindi publish benchmarks naming the GPUs, models, and baseline engines behind its "fastest" claim?
Does the project-maya CUDA+ROCm pull request merge, and what workload and baseline produce the 48% figure?
Does an independent benchmark compare mixed NVIDIA+AMD inference against a single-vendor setup at equal cost?
Does ML Drift add server-side or LLM-scale support, or stay on-device only?
Does the AMD HIP inference server publish throughput and model-support numbers against vLLM on ROCm?
